Thinking of hiring a company for SEO, AEO & GEO?

Don’t choose one just because they offer the lowest price or promise “#1 rankings.”

Before signing the contract, ask these questions 👇
1️⃣ Do they understand your business?
Your strategy should start with your industry, audience, competitors, services and business goals, not just a list of keywords.
2️⃣ Do they have a proper SEO strategy?
Technical SEO, content, on-page optimisation, internal linking, authority building, local SEO and conversion optimisation all matter.
3️⃣ What exactly are they doing for AEO?
AEO isn't simply adding FAQs to your website. It’s about creating content that clearly answers the questions your potential customers are asking.
4️⃣ Do they understand GEO & AI Search?
Ask them how they plan to improve your visibility across AI-driven search experiences such as ChatGPT, Gemini and other platforms.
And be careful of anyone promising “guaranteed ChatGPT rankings.”
5️⃣ How will they measure results?
Don't settle for a monthly keyword report.
Look at:
-Search visibility
- Organic traffic
-AI/answer visibility
- Brand mentions & citations
- Qualified enquiries
- Conversions
- ROI

6️⃣ Who is actually working on your account?
SEO isn't performed by a single magic tool.
Understand the team behind your strategy, SEO specialists, content writers, developers, strategists and other resources required for execution.
7️⃣ Can they show real case studies?
Don't just ask for screenshots of keywords ranking #1.
Ask:
- Where did the client start?
- What was done?
- What changed?
And what business impact did it create?

8️⃣ Do they understand your business ROI?
Because ultimately:
- Ranking is not the goal.
- Visibility is not the goal.
- Traffic is not the goal.
- The real goal is business growth.

So before you compare agencies based on ₹10K vs ₹50K vs ₹1L per month, compare the strategy, team, execution, scope and expected business outcome.

The cheapest SEO company isn't necessarily expensive.
And the most expensive one isn't necessarily the best.

The right question is:
“What am I actually getting for what I'm paying?”

Interviewer asked me "How can we conduct contract testing using Playwright?" 

First correction I had to do: We cannot conduct contract testing as it natively cannot hold "consumer" & "provider" contracts. But we can explore "json-schema" validations. Which is the next best!

To understand json-schema validation we need 4 steps: 
1) Access to API spec (API Contract)
2) Create Json Schema (generate json schema using: )
3) Store json schema in your framework 
4) Use AJV/ZOD to compile schema and validate with response/request body used/received after execution of API test.

Always remember: JSON Schema validation is one technique used inside contract testing. It is not a synonym for contract testing itself.

What it covers: field presence, data types, required versus optional fields, string formats, nested structure. All of this is expressed once, declaratively, in a schema file.

What it cannot do: 

1) It cannot verify the HTTP status code or response headers were correct.
 
2) It cannot check semantic or business rules a type system cannot express, for example that end_date comes after start_date, or that a total matches the sum of line items.
 
3) It cannot tell you whether the schema reflects a real, agreed contract, or just whatever the API happened to return the one time it was sampled.

Quick tip: If you review the API spec carefully after every change made by Backend teams. Then we can use: "toJsonSchema" to dynamically generate schema using a flag. 
If set to true, it updates the schema files and we just validate the final playwright report.

Ema does not charge per seat or per token. It gets paid when the task is finished.

The company runs teams of AI agents across HR, IT and finance work, and this week raised $77 million in a Series B led by Creaegis, TechCrunch reported. Its customers include Google, Microsoft, PwC and KPMG. According to TechCrunch, Ema ties its pricing to completed tasks and business outcomes rather than seats or tokens.

The billing model decides who carries the risk when an agent fails.

Under a seat licence, you pay whether anyone uses the tool or not. Under token pricing, you pay for every attempt, including the ones that go nowhere. Either way the vendor is paid for access, and the failed run is your cost.

Pay per finished task and that cost goes back to the vendor. The agent that stalls halfway through a workflow becomes their problem.

Ema says more than 90% of its customers have expanded beyond their first use case, and that revenue has grown 50-fold in two years. It does not say how much of that is down to the pricing.

The model will not suit every job. Someone has to agree in advance what "finished" means, and that definition is where these contracts get argued over.

It still gives any business a sharper question for the next vendor quoting on AI work: when the task does not complete, who pays for it?

Ask us too. A vendor worth hiring will have the answer ready.

Ninety-five percent of insider cases are not a villain. They are a file that was never closed.

Aviv Nahum’s Forbes Technology Council note is written for security teams, but the operational ask sits with HR as much as with the SOC. Insider risk, he writes, grows with every name added to the org chart. Most of it is not theft. About 95 percent of cases are negligence or error. The rest is a mix of malice and stolen credentials. Traditional DLP is a static rule that a 4.9 MB file walks past. UEBA flags anomalies and then floods the queue. The window that still concentrates harm is the departing employee: recruiter contact, an accepted offer, a last week with residual access. He also flags a newer class. Synthetic users, AI agents that act with employee-like permissions, will break the same static policies. His prescription is not “watch everyone.” It is concentrate on people who hold high-value data, give the problem a single owner, and treat it as a joint brief for security, HR and legal.

That brief starts before the badge is cut. Who is this person. What did the last employer confirm. What sits in the integrity file. The same brief runs again on the last day. Collect the kit. Kill the identity on every repository, not only the SSO tile. An AI monitor that reasons on behaviour is useful after the fact. It does not replace a source letter at hire and a closed kit at exit.

Absolute People Screen’s work is that letter. Employment verification tests the roles and dates that travel with the CV. Identity checks test whether the person on the contract is the person on the badge. Integrity screening looks for prior trade-secret, laptop-retention and adverse-media files a clean operations profile can hide. Used together they give CHRO, CPO, compliance and corporate security leaders a start file and a stop file, which is the part of insider risk that hiring still owns.

If the offer is accepted elsewhere, close the folder before the last Friday.

A lot of companies are sending their teams for AI training while the leadership team skips it. I understand why. Leaders are busy, and the assumption is they only need to know enough to approve the budget.

The problem is that agentic AI budgets are now being approved by people who haven't used these tools on their own work. So when a vendor says "the agent handles exceptions," nobody in the room knows what to ask next. 
What does it actually do when it's unsure? 
Where does that case go? 
Who checks it? 

These aren't technical questions. They decide whether the thing works in production and who carries the risk when it doesn't.

Our last hiring batch was run by AI agents. I was comfortable signing off on that because I had used these tools enough to know where they get things wrong and where a human check was needed. Without that, I would have been approving it on trust.

If you're approving AI spend, you need enough hands-on exposure to question the plan yourself. You don't need to build agents. You do need to know which decisions should stay with a person, and what you expect to stop spending on if this works. If nobody on the leadership team can answer those two, that's a training gap. It's cheaper to fix before the contract is signed than after.

🔐 Digital Due Diligence: The 5-Minute Habit That Could Save You From a Nightmare

We do due diligence before signing a contract, hiring someone, or making an investment. But how often do we do it for our own digital identity?

Take 10 minutes this week to check these:
✅ Passwords — Are you still using the one you set 3 years ago? Rotate passwords regularly, and never reuse the same one across accounts.

✅ 2FA (Two-Factor Authentication) — Enable it everywhere: Facebook, Instagram, X, LinkedIn, Gmail, and yes — even your ChatGPT and Claude accounts. AI tools now hold your conversations, documents, and sometimes business data. If someone gets in, it's not just an inbox they access — it's your voice, your identity, your credibility.

✅ Device updates — That "Update available" notification you keep dismissing? It's often a security patch closing a door hackers are already knocking on.

✅ Login alerts — Turn on notifications for new device logins. It's the fastest way to catch unauthorized access before real damage is done.

⚠️ Why this matters: A hijacked social or AI account isn't just inconvenient — it opens the door to impersonation, scams targeting your network, and social engineering attacks that exploit the trust people have in you.

Cybersecurity isn't only an IT department's job. It's personal due diligence — and it takes less time than scrolling your feed for 5 minutes.

Have you checked your 2FA settings this month? 👇

By 2028, operations and finance heads will own AI failure liability on their balance sheets and performance reviews.

Most mid-career professionals still assume IT will absorb AI compliance and model error risks because IT buys the software licenses. That assumption seems logical at first glance.

It is also wrong. IT maintains the infrastructure, but IT cannot spot accounting errors, contract misinterpretations, or compliance hallucinations in daily business outputs. Domain judgment belongs entirely to functional leaders.

Job markets already reflect this shift. In an analysis of executive job listings, operational AI governance now appears in 34% of non-technical director roles, up from 8% two years ago.

I would change my mind if enterprise budgets showed IT departments hiring accounting and operations specialists to audit prompt outputs. Enterprise budgets show the exact opposite.

This quarter, stop waiting for an IT policy. Document the verification checks and audit controls on the automated tools your team uses today. You do not need to write code to govern business risk.

If an automated workflow in your department produces a compliant-looking error tomorrow, who does your board call: your IT director, or you?

About 18 months ago, I was caught in the federal workforce cuts under DOGE. Trying to get back into legal support as a paralegal has been tough, automated screenings, quiet hiring, and the steady creep of AI handling contract triage and routine drafting have clearly squeezed the market.

While looking for other options, I ended up stepping into remote AI training. For anyone who hasn’t seen this corner of the internet, it’s often listed as prompt evaluation, RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback), or data annotation. In plain English: you test AI models, write prompts, evaluate and edit outputs, and grade responses for accuracy, reasoning, and tone. It does not require a computer science degree. The skills needed are strong reading comprehension, sharp research instincts, attention to detail, and clear writing, backgrounds that a lot of paralegals, former federal workers, educators, and administrative pros already bring to the table.  

The catch is how the work actually operates. You aren’t hired by one company; work is scattered across dozens of third-party platforms (like Outlier, DataAnnotation, Mercor, Mindrift, and others). Because of that setup, it cannot be treated as reliable, steady income. Projects start and stop with zero notice, pay rates can shift, and accounts can go dry without clear feedback. As a flexible bridge or supplemental income, though, it helps: general evaluation usually pays around $18–$25/hr, while specialized domain work (like legal, technical, or finance) can pay $35–$60+/hr depending on active client demand. Some projects offer significantly greater compensation to people with specialized skills like law, finance or coding.

Because doing this solo across disconnected dashboards is isolating, a few of us started an independent, worker-led community on Discord and Reddit. We’re just colleagues comparing notes, sharing vetted platform leads, helping each other navigate complex onboarding guidelines, and keeping each other sane in this job market. The group is completely free, no courses, no coaching fees, and no upsells. 

We also welcome tech recruiters and hiring teams. Many of our members carry solid backgrounds in technical writing, QA, data operations, paralegal analysis, and development, and a lot of folks are looking for dependable, permanent work. Recruiters are free to join and post openings directly.  

If you’re trying to navigate this market, curious about how AI training works, or just want a grounded network of peers, leave a reply below and I’ll send you an invite to the Discord.

Boring Accountant at the Coffee shop.

Piyush Gupta, SMU chairman and former DBS chief, told Kang Wan Chern that the graduate premium will shrink. If AI gives a school-leaver the same knowledge as a graduate, employers stop paying extra for the degree. His advice to students: forget one major, take ten minors, and learn to judge whether an answer makes sense.

Then Vikram Khanna published the numbers. Retrenchments in the second quarter were the highest since the pandemic, in an economy growing at 5.9 per cent. The hardest hit were not the low-skilled. They were PMETs, degree holders and workers in their fifties. Only half the degree holders found a job within six months. Cleaners and labourers did better, at seven in ten.

Did Gupta described the future and Vikram showed it has arrived??? Wow!!!

I need to be honest here, because this cuts against something I have believed since I was a teenager. I was sent to Singapore alone at 13. From then on, I believed professional qualifications were how you protected yourself. I chased every one I could. At my "old" age, I am still at it, doing a doctorate.  

Was I wrong? Don't think so. Never stop learning but may need to be re-tune to Mr Gupta's Prescription.

The credential may opens the door. It has never been what keeps you in the room. What keeps you in the room is the ten minors: the tax person who understands cash flow, the accountant who can read a contract, the CFO who can sit with a founder and say "here is what these numbers mean, and here is what I would do."

Three things I take from this week so far:-
- If you are 50-plus with a good degree and a senior title, you are now the vulnerable group. Not the cleaner. You. Act before the letter arrives, not after.
- Stack sideways, not upward. Another certificate in the same field buys you nothing. A skill from a different field buys you a second door.
- To employers: keep hiring juniors. Gupta's point about DBS applies to a five-person firm. Stop hiring graduates today and you have no reviewers in five years. But economically and technologically, it is getting more and more difficult to even justify grooming "reviewers".

Everything I built, I built on qualifications. Perhaps this worked for someone starting 30 years ago. But if I were 25 today, I would collect skills the way I collected certificates.

Day 1 of the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity CMO Accelerator in LA had plenty of AI on the agenda. But the idea I kept writing down was about control, and how little of it we actually have.

A few lines that stuck with me:

🎁 "Adding value is simply giving people what they are not expecting." Luiz Sanches, Kimberly-Clark

Most marketing gives people exactly what they expect. Then we act surprised when they skip it.

🌯 "Today, real is much more defined by what people talk about you than what the brand talks about itself." Fernando Machado, Chipotle Mexican Grill

Chipotle is acting on this. They opened their kitchens to 100 creators and let them film what they found.

💡 "Never sit on ideas. Good idea is idea on the street, not on a PowerPoint." Fernando again, on his house rules for the team

I know a few decks that could use this as a cover slide. Mine included.

🤝 "The second that you're checking a contract, did this person miss their quarterly social post? You're dead." Michael D. Ratner, on talent partnerships

🧭 "You cannot make people stay with you. They need to want to stay with you." Olga Osminkina - Jones, on leading a team through AI change

It's the same lesson, pointed inward.

🏈 Then there was Lara Krug, CMO of the Kansas City Chiefs, who may have less control than anyone in the room. League rules keep the Chiefs from advertising outside a 75-mile radius of the stadium. So they let fans everywhere else tell the story, and they now have roughly 10 times more TikTok followers than Kansas City has residents. She can't control injuries, headlines or the score either. So what she hires for is curiosity, humility and what she called "figure it outableness." When her team brings her something nobody has done before, she tells them there's no page in the playbook for it and they'll work it out together.

"Figure it outableness" is a real word now. I'm hiring for it.

When a customer asks AI about your product, they get a sales rep who keeps pointing at the competitor's shelf.

📌 My takeaway: your brand is increasingly written by other people. That includes creators, fans, talent, your own team and now machines. The job is less about controlling the message and more about deserving a good one.

Day 2 tomorrow.

Same two-panel structure as the reference, rebuilt in your palette and typefaces so it sits alongside your other posts. 2040x2550, LinkedIn's 4:5 portrait.
I credited Travis Thompson and Modern Data 101 in the footer. The layer model and the elevation chart are their framing, and reposting it unattributed is the kind of thing data people notice and comment on. With the credit, it reads as you engaging with good work rather than lifting it.
The bottom row is where I made it yours — three staffing takeaways the original doesn't have: rewrite the req rather than the title, test thinking over keywords, and buy the capability before the headcount. That last one is the commercial point, and it's true rather than salesy.
Here's the caption:
Most teams are still hiring for the 2023 version of their data team.
The work didn't disappear. It moved up.
Pipeline plumbing, standard reports and boilerplate code are getting automated — that's the commodity layer. What's expanding above it is the irreducibly human part: judgment, context, architectural thinking, accountability.
So the same three roles now point somewhere different:
Data Engineer → Systems Architect for agentic infrastructure
 Data Analyst → Decision Intelligence Specialist
 Data Scientist → ML Engineer, or Decision Scientist
And a set of capabilities nobody had a title for two years ago now has to live somewhere on the team: context engineering at the infrastructure layer, semantic architecture and data product management at the logic layer, AI data quality, agent workflow design and governance at the execution layer.
These aren't six people you post reqs for tomorrow. They're six things that have to be owned by someone, and most teams currently own two.
What this changes about hiring:
→ A job description copied from 2023 screens for tools. The work that's left screens for architectural judgment. That's a different interview and a different shortlist.
 → Ask a candidate how they'd handle a specific failure mode, not whether they've "worked with" the platform. The gap between those two questions is where mis-hires now come from.
 → Most of these are 9–18 month needs, not permanent seats. Contract specialists can cover the shift while your core team grows into it.
Hiring for data or AI this quarter and unsure which of these you're actually missing? That's usually a short conversation.

A multinational company can buy one AI tool and inherit many legal problems. The model may be trained by a vendor in one country, hosted in another, used by employees across regions, and affect customers or workers in several jurisdictions. That is the hard part of AI governance now. The risk no longer sits only with the team that built or bought the system. It sits across procurement, privacy, legal, security, compliance, product, and operations. The EU AI Act pushes companies toward a structured, risk-based compliance model with clear obligations and strict penalties. The United States is moving through a more fragmented path, with state laws, sector rules, and agency enforcement all shaping expectations. At the same time, many enterprises rely on third-party algorithms they do not fully control.

Regulatory divergence is now an operating model problem
For multinational enterprises, AI compliance is no longer a single legal review before launch. It is an operating model problem. The EU AI Act sets a broad framework for AI systems placed on the EU market or used in ways that affect people in the EU. Its core structure is risk-based. Some AI practices are prohibited. High-risk AI systems face requirements around risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, cybersecurity, and post-market monitoring. The law also matters beyond companies headquartered in Europe. A business based in the United States or Asia may still fall within scope if its AI system is used in the EU or if outputs affect people in the EU.

The United States looks different. There is no single federal AI law that mirrors the EU AI Act or the GDPR. Instead, companies must track a mix of rules and enforcement sources, including:
- State privacy laws that address automated decision-making, profiling, and consumer rights
- Employment rules affecting hiring tools and workplace monitoring
- Sector laws for credit, housing, insurance, health, education, and financial services
- Consumer protection enforcement from agencies such as the Federal Trade Commission
- Civil rights and anti-discrimination rules enforced by federal and state agencies
- Local rules, such as laws covering automated employment decision tools
That means a system considered high-risk in Europe may trigger a formal EU AI Act compliance while the US require separate analysis under state, employment law, anti-discrimination law, and sector-specific rules.

#Hiring: Senior Data Scientist – AI/ML

📍 Location: Remote
💼 Experience: 7+ Years
📌 Employment: C2C / Contract
🕐 Shift: IST
⏳ Duration: Minimum 1 Year
✈️ Travel: Occasional 2–3 days to Bangalore, if required

We are looking for a strong Senior Data Scientist / ML Expert with hands-on expertise in Core Machine Learning and Data Science to work on global Media Optimization initiatives.

🔹 Key Responsibilities
• Develop and manage end-to-end Machine Learning & Data Science models
• Analyze data, identify trends, and generate actionable insights
• Adapt and scale ML models across markets and business requirements
• Work on Media Optimization / Media Analytics use cases
• Develop predictive models, forecasting solutions, and other ML applications
• Create visualizations to communicate model results and business impact
• Present solutions to technical and business stakeholders
• Collaborate with global and cross-functional teams

🔹 Must-Have Skills
✅ Strong Core ML & Data Science experience
✅ Hands-on Python, R & SQL
✅ Predictive Modeling, Forecasting & Model Evaluation
✅ Experience with AWS / GCP / Databricks / Snowflake / Azure
✅ GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket
✅ Jupyter Notebook / JupyterLab
✅ Strong communication and stakeholder management skills
✅ Ability to translate business problems into scalable ML solutions

🔹 Good to Have
• Media Optimization / Media Analytics experience
• Tableau / Power BI / Domo
• Generative AI / GenAI exposure
• Experience working with global teams and adapting models across markets

📩 Candidate Details
Name | Contact | Email | LinkedIn | Total Exp | Relevant Exp | Current Company | Location | Current CTC | Expected CTC | Notice Period/LWD

📧 Apply: sanjana.a@martinettechnologies.com

🔁 Follow • Share • Refer • Tag suitable candidates!

🔹 Job Type: Contract
🔹 Experience: 15+ Years
🔑 Must-Have Skills:
• Treasure Data / Treasure Data CDP – Production experience is strongly preferred
• Enterprise ETL/ELT, Data Warehousing & Lakehouse architecture
• Strong hands-on Python & SQL
• Real-time analytics, event-driven architecture & streaming pipelines
• Hands-on Apache Kafka
• CDC / Debezium / incremental data processing
• Snowflake / Databricks
• AWS, Azure, or GCP cloud data engineering
• Batch + real-time enterprise data architecture
🤖 Generative AI / Modern Data:
• AI-ready data pipelines
• RAG & Vector Databases
• LangChain / LangGraph / LlamaIndex
• AI Agents

Priority: Treasure Data + Real-Time Analytics + Enterprise ETL/Data Warehouse, ideally combined with Kafka + Generative AI experience.
📩 Interested candidates can send me : sivak@connecttechtalent.com
